```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 8, fig.height = 3.6, dpi = 120)
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(readr); library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(stringr)
  library(ggplot2); library(knitr)
})
options(dplyr.summarise.inform = FALSE)

# ---- helpers ----------------------------------------------------------------
fmt <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
pct <- function(a, b) sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * a / b)
tbl <- function(df, n = 30, caption = NULL) {
  df <- as.data.frame(df)
  if (nrow(df) > n) caption <- paste0(c(caption, sprintf("(first %d of %d rows)", n, nrow(df))), collapse = " ")
  kable(head(df, n), format.args = list(big.mark = ","), caption = caption, digits = 2)
}
profile_columns <- function(df) {
  tibble(column = names(df),
         type = vapply(df, function(x) class(x)[1], character(1)),
         n_missing = vapply(df, function(x) sum(is.na(x)), integer(1)),
         pct_missing = round(100 * n_missing / nrow(df), 2),
         n_distinct = vapply(df, function(x) n_distinct(x, na.rm = TRUE), integer(1)),
         example = vapply(df, function(x) as.character(x[which(!is.na(x))[1]]), character(1)))
}
numeric_summary <- function(df) {
  df %>% select(where(is.numeric)) %>%
    pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable") %>%
    group_by(variable) %>%
    summarise(n_na = sum(is.na(value)), min = min(value, na.rm = TRUE),
              p01 = quantile(value, .01, na.rm = TRUE), median = median(value, na.rm = TRUE),
              mean = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE), p99 = quantile(value, .99, na.rm = TRUE),
              max = max(value, na.rm = TRUE), n_zero = sum(value == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
              n_neg = sum(value < 0, na.rm = TRUE))
}
freq <- function(df, ...) df %>% count(..., sort = TRUE) %>% mutate(pct = round(100 * n / sum(n), 2))
key_info <- function(df, cols) {
  n_keys <- nrow(distinct(df, across(all_of(cols))))
  tibble(key = paste(cols, collapse = " + "), rows = nrow(df), distinct = n_keys,
         extra_rows = nrow(df) - n_keys, unique = n_keys == nrow(df))
}
check_fk <- function(child, child_name, parent, parent_name, by) {
  tibble(relationship = sprintf("%s.%s → %s", child_name, by, parent_name),
         child_rows = nrow(child),
         unmatched_rows = sum(!child[[by]] %in% parent[[by]]),
         unmatched_keys = n_distinct(child[[by]][!child[[by]] %in% parent[[by]]]),
         parents_without_child = sum(!unique(parent[[by]]) %in% child[[by]]))
}

# ---- chart style: one hue, recessive grid, ink-coloured text ----------------
col_main <- "#2a78d6"; ink <- "#52514e"
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.y = element_line(colour = "#e6e5e1", linewidth = 0.3),
        axis.text = element_text(colour = ink), axis.title = element_text(colour = ink),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12), plot.title.position = "plot",
        plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = ink)))
```

# Purpose and approach {.unnumbered}

This document explores all seven Aurora Market tables before any cleaning. For each table we check its **dimensions and unit of observation**, **identifiers**, **missing values**, **duplicates**, **unusual numeric or categorical values**, and other **consistency issues**. We then look at **how the tables connect**. Nothing here modifies the data; every number is computed from the original CSV files in `Data/`.

The same analysis is available as a console script in `R/02_data_familiarization.R`.

# Loading the data

Every column gets an explicit type. All `*_timestamp` columns and `shipping_deadline` are parsed as UTC date-times, as the README requires.

```{r load}
dt <- col_datetime(format = "")
spec <- list(
  customers = cols(.default = col_character()),
  orders = cols(.default = col_character(),
                purchase_timestamp = dt, approval_timestamp = dt, carrier_timestamp = dt,
                delivery_timestamp = dt, estimated_delivery_timestamp = dt),
  order_items = cols(.default = col_character(), item_number = col_integer(),
                     shipping_deadline = dt, item_price = col_double(), freight_cost = col_double()),
  products = cols(.default = col_double(), product_id = col_character(), product_category = col_character()),
  sellers = cols(.default = col_character()),
  payments = cols(.default = col_character(), payment_sequence = col_integer(),
                  installments = col_integer(), payment_amount = col_double()),
  customer_feedback = cols(.default = col_character(), rating = col_integer(),
                           has_title = col_logical(), has_comment = col_logical(),
                           comment_length = col_integer(),
                           feedback_created_timestamp = dt, feedback_answered_timestamp = dt))

d <- lapply(names(spec), function(t) read_csv(file.path("Data", paste0(t, ".csv")),
                                              col_types = spec[[t]], na = c("", "NA")))
names(d) <- names(spec)
customers <- d$customers; orders <- d$orders; items <- d$order_items
products <- d$products; sellers <- d$sellers; payments <- d$payments; feedback <- d$customer_feedback

parse_issues <- vapply(d, function(x) nrow(problems(x)), integer(1))
```

Parsing problems across all tables: **`r sum(parse_issues)`**. Every value matched its declared type.

# Overview of the seven tables

```{r overview}
overview <- tibble(
  table = names(d),
  rows = vapply(d, nrow, integer(1)),
  columns = vapply(d, ncol, integer(1)),
  cells_missing = vapply(d, function(x) sum(is.na(x)), integer(1)),
  exact_duplicate_rows = vapply(d, function(x) sum(duplicated(x)), integer(1)),
  unit_of_observation = c("customer record (one per order)", "order", "item line within an order",
                          "product listing", "seller", "payment within an order", "feedback record"))
tbl(overview)
```

The tables are at **different units of observation**. Only `orders` and `customers` share the same grain, and three tables (`order_items`, `payments`, `customer_feedback`) can have several rows per order.

# customers

```{r cust-structure}
tbl(profile_columns(customers), caption = "Column profile")
```

## Identifiers

```{r cust-keys}
rec_per_cust <- customers %>% count(customer_id, name = "records")
n_multi <- sum(rec_per_cust$records > 1)
tbl(bind_rows(key_info(customers, "customer_record_id"), key_info(customers, "customer_id")))
tbl(rec_per_cust %>% count(records, name = "customers") %>% mutate(pct = round(100 * customers / sum(customers), 2)),
    caption = "Records per customer_id")
```

`customer_record_id` is unique, but **`customer_id` is not**. `r fmt(n_multi)` people (`r pct(n_multi, nrow(rec_per_cust))`) have more than one record, and one has `r max(rec_per_cust$records)`. As Section 4 shows, a *record* is created per order. Customer-level questions (repeat purchase, lifetime value) must therefore group by `customer_id`.

```{r cust-location}
loc <- customers %>% semi_join(filter(rec_per_cust, records > 1), by = "customer_id") %>%
  group_by(customer_id) %>%
  summarise(postal = n_distinct(postal_area), city = n_distinct(city), region = n_distinct(region))
pa_city  <- customers %>% distinct(postal_area, city) %>% count(postal_area) %>% filter(n > 1)
city_reg <- customers %>% distinct(city, region) %>% count(city) %>% filter(n > 1)
```

**Location is stored per record, not per person.** Of the `r fmt(nrow(loc))` repeat customers, `r sum(loc$postal > 1)` change postal area, `r sum(loc$city > 1)` change city and `r sum(loc$region > 1)` change region between records. It most likely reflects the delivery address of each order.

**Geography hierarchy.** There are `r fmt(n_distinct(customers$postal_area))` postal areas, `r fmt(n_distinct(customers$city))` cities and `r n_distinct(customers$region)` regions. Each postal area maps to a single city (`r nrow(pa_city)` exceptions). However, **`r nrow(city_reg)` city identifiers appear in more than one region**, so city codes are not safe as a standalone geographic key.

```{r cust-region}
reg <- freq(customers, region)
tbl(reg, n = 10, caption = "Customer records by region")
```

Customers are highly concentrated: `r reg$region[1]` alone holds **`r reg$pct[1]`%** of records, and the smallest regions have fewer than 100. Region-level estimates for small regions will be imprecise.

# orders

```{r ord-structure}
tbl(profile_columns(orders), caption = "Column profile")
tbl(bind_rows(key_info(orders, "order_id"), key_info(orders, "customer_record_id")))
```

Both `order_id` and `customer_record_id` are unique here. Orders and customer records are therefore **1:1**.

## Order status and structured missingness

```{r ord-status}
miss_status <- orders %>% group_by(order_status) %>%
  summarise(orders = n(), no_approval = sum(is.na(approval_timestamp)),
            no_carrier = sum(is.na(carrier_timestamp)), no_delivery = sum(is.na(delivery_timestamp))) %>%
  arrange(desc(orders)) %>% mutate(pct_orders = round(100 * orders / sum(orders), 2), .after = orders)
tbl(miss_status)
cmp_no_del <- sum(orders$order_status == "COMPLETED" & is.na(orders$delivery_timestamp))
canc_del   <- sum(orders$order_status == "CANCELLED" & !is.na(orders$delivery_timestamp))
```

`r pct(sum(orders$order_status == "COMPLETED"), nrow(orders))` of orders are COMPLETED. Missing timestamps are **not random**: they follow the order status. An order that never shipped has no carrier or delivery date. Missing delivery dates are therefore meaningful information, not a cleaning problem to drop. There are small contradictions: `r cmp_no_del` COMPLETED orders have no delivery date, and `r canc_del` CANCELLED orders have one.

## Time coverage

```{r ord-time, fig.height = 3.2}
monthly <- orders %>% count(month = as.Date(format(purchase_timestamp, "%Y-%m-01")))
monthly <- tibble(month = seq(min(monthly$month), max(monthly$month), by = "month")) %>%
  left_join(monthly, by = "month") %>% mutate(n = coalesce(n, 0L))
thin <- monthly %>% filter(n < 100)
ggplot(monthly, aes(month, n)) +
  geom_col(fill = col_main, width = 25) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .05))) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "3 months", date_labels = "%b %y") +
  labs(title = "Orders per month", subtitle = "Sparse first months and an abrupt end in Oct 2024",
       x = NULL, y = "Orders")
```

Purchases run from `r format(min(orders$purchase_timestamp), "%d %b %Y")` to `r format(max(orders$purchase_timestamp), "%d %b %Y")`. Months with fewer than 100 orders: `r paste0(format(thin$month, "%b %Y"), " (", thin$n, ")", collapse = ", ")`. These edge months are not comparable to the rest and should probably be excluded from any trend or seasonal analysis. There is also a visible peak in December 2023.

## Chronological consistency

```{r ord-seq}
seq_checks <- tibble(
  check = c("approval before purchase", "carrier handover before approval",
            "carrier handover before purchase", "delivery before carrier handover",
            "delivery before purchase", "estimated delivery before purchase"),
  orders = c(sum(orders$approval_timestamp < orders$purchase_timestamp, na.rm = TRUE),
             sum(orders$carrier_timestamp < orders$approval_timestamp, na.rm = TRUE),
             sum(orders$carrier_timestamp < orders$purchase_timestamp, na.rm = TRUE),
             sum(orders$delivery_timestamp < orders$carrier_timestamp, na.rm = TRUE),
             sum(orders$delivery_timestamp < orders$purchase_timestamp, na.rm = TRUE),
             sum(orders$estimated_delivery_timestamp < orders$purchase_timestamp, na.rm = TRUE)))
tbl(seq_checks)
```

The order lifecycle should run purchase → approval → carrier → delivery. **`r fmt(seq_checks$orders[2])` orders reach the carrier before approval** and `r seq_checks$orders[3]` before the purchase itself. This matters for any variable built from stage durations, such as "seller handling time".

## Delivery performance

```{r ord-delivery}
del <- orders %>% filter(!is.na(delivery_timestamp)) %>%
  mutate(delivery_days = as.numeric(difftime(delivery_timestamp, purchase_timestamp, units = "days")),
         promised_days = as.numeric(difftime(estimated_delivery_timestamp, purchase_timestamp, units = "days")),
         days_vs_estimate = as.numeric(difftime(delivery_timestamp, estimated_delivery_timestamp, units = "days")))
late_time <- mean(del$days_vs_estimate > 0)
late_date <- mean(as.Date(del$delivery_timestamp) > as.Date(del$estimated_delivery_timestamp))
tbl(numeric_summary(select(del, delivery_days, promised_days, days_vs_estimate)))
```

```{r ord-delivery-plot, fig.height = 3.2}
ggplot(del, aes(as.numeric(as.Date(delivery_timestamp) - as.Date(estimated_delivery_timestamp)))) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, boundary = 0, fill = col_main, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = ink, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-50, 40)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .05))) +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = Inf, label = "late", hjust = 0, vjust = 1.5, colour = ink, size = 3.5) +
  labs(title = "Delivery date minus estimated date (days)",
       subtitle = "Most orders arrive well before the estimate; the late tail is small but long",
       x = "Days (negative = early)", y = "Orders")
```

The median delivery takes **`r round(median(del$delivery_days), 1)` days**, against a median promise of `r round(median(del$promised_days), 1)` days. The estimate is always recorded at 00:00, so it is a *date*, while the actual delivery has a precise time. Comparing raw timestamps labels `r pct(late_time, 1)` of orders late. Comparing calendar dates gives **`r pct(late_date, 1)`**. A "late" variable should be built from dates.

# order_items

```{r it-structure}
tbl(profile_columns(items), caption = "Column profile")
```

## Identifiers and duplicates

```{r it-keys}
n_exact <- sum(duplicated(items))
dup_keys <- items %>% group_by(order_id, item_number) %>% filter(n() > 1) %>% ungroup()
tbl(key_info(items, c("order_id", "item_number")))
tbl(head(dup_keys, 4), caption = "Example of duplicated item lines")
numbering <- items %>% distinct(order_id, item_number) %>% group_by(order_id) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), mx = max(item_number), mn = min(item_number))
```

The intended key (`order_id`, `item_number`) is **not unique**. There are `r n_exact` exact duplicate rows, identical in every column. Section 8.2 shows that payments match the totals *without* these duplicates, so they are recording errors. Item numbers otherwise run 1…n with no gaps (`r sum(numbering$mx != numbering$n | numbering$mn != 1)` exceptions).

## Order composition

```{r it-composition}
per_order <- items %>% distinct() %>% group_by(order_id) %>%
  summarise(items = n(), products = n_distinct(product_id), sellers = n_distinct(seller_id))
tbl(freq(per_order, items) %>% arrange(items), n = 8, caption = "Item lines per order")
```

`r pct(sum(per_order$items == 1), nrow(per_order))` of orders contain a single item. `r fmt(sum(per_order$sellers > 1))` orders (`r pct(sum(per_order$sellers > 1), nrow(per_order))`) involve more than one seller. In `r fmt(sum(per_order$items > per_order$products))` orders the same product appears on several lines. There is no quantity column; **quantity is represented by repeated lines**.

## Prices, freight and shipping deadlines

```{r it-prices}
sd <- items %>% distinct() %>% left_join(select(orders, order_id, purchase_timestamp), by = "order_id") %>%
  mutate(deadline_days = as.numeric(difftime(shipping_deadline, purchase_timestamp, units = "days")))
tbl(numeric_summary(bind_cols(select(items %>% distinct(), item_price, freight_cost), select(sd, deadline_days))))
```

- Prices are **strongly right-skewed**: the median is `r round(median(items$item_price), 2)` and the maximum `r fmt(max(items$item_price))`. Log transformations or robust statistics will be needed.
- `r fmt(sum(items$freight_cost == 0))` item lines have zero freight, and `r fmt(sum(items$freight_cost > items$item_price))` (`r pct(sum(items$freight_cost > items$item_price), nrow(items))`) have freight higher than the item price.
- The shipping deadline is normally 2–19 days after purchase, but `r sum(sd$deadline_days > 30)` lines have deadlines over 30 days away, with a maximum of **`r round(max(sd$deadline_days))` days**. These are likely entry errors.

# products

```{r pr-structure}
tbl(profile_columns(products), caption = "Column profile")
tbl(key_info(products, "product_id"))
```

## Missing values come in one block

```{r pr-missing}
tbl(products %>%
  transmute(category_missing = is.na(product_category),
            listing_info_missing = is.na(name_length) & is.na(description_length) & is.na(photo_count),
            dimensions_missing = is.na(weight_g) & is.na(length_cm) & is.na(height_cm) & is.na(width_cm)) %>%
  count(category_missing, listing_info_missing, dimensions_missing))
```

The category, name length, description length and photo count are missing **together for the same `r sum(is.na(products$product_category))` products**. That is one missing-data pattern (listings created without metadata), not four separate problems. Only `r sum(is.na(products$weight_g))` products lack physical dimensions.

## Category labels are inconsistently spelled

```{r pr-categories}
normalise_cat <- function(x) {
  x %>% toupper() %>% str_replace_all("[^A-Z]+", "_") %>% str_replace_all("_+", "_") %>%
    str_replace_all("^_|_$", "") %>% str_replace("^HOUSEHOLDGOODS$", "HOUSEHOLD_GOODS")
}
cat_map <- products %>% filter(!is.na(product_category)) %>% distinct(product_category) %>%
  mutate(normalised = normalise_cat(product_category))
tbl(cat_map %>% group_by(normalised) %>% filter(n() > 1) %>% arrange(normalised) %>%
      left_join(count(products, product_category, name = "products"), by = "product_category"),
    caption = "Labels that refer to the same category")
```

There are **`r nrow(cat_map)` raw labels but only `r n_distinct(cat_map$normalised)` real categories**. Five categories also appear in variant spellings: lowercase, hyphens, spaces, doubled or missing underscores. Each variant holds exactly 24 products, which suggests they were introduced deliberately and must be harmonised before any category analysis.

```{r pr-cat-dist}
tbl(products %>% mutate(category = normalise_cat(product_category)) %>% freq(category), n = 10,
    caption = "Top categories after harmonising")
```

## Physical attributes

```{r pr-numeric}
tbl(numeric_summary(select(products, -product_id, -product_category)))
tbl(products %>% arrange(desc(weight_g)) %>%
      mutate(volume_litres = length_cm * height_cm * width_cm / 1000) %>%
      select(product_id, product_category, weight_g, length_cm, height_cm, width_cm, volume_litres) %>% head(8),
    caption = "Heaviest products")
big <- sum(products$weight_g > 100000, na.rm = TRUE)
```

`weight_g` contains `r sum(products$weight_g == 0, na.rm = TRUE)` zero weights. It also contains **`r big` products over 100 kg packed in boxes no larger than about 55 cm per side**, the heaviest at 9,375,000 g (9.4 tonnes). The 99.9th percentile is only `r fmt(quantile(products$weight_g, .999, na.rm = TRUE))` g, so these are almost certainly entry errors. They would dominate any analysis of weight and freight.

# sellers

```{r se-structure}
tbl(profile_columns(sellers), caption = "Column profile")
tbl(key_info(sellers, "seller_id"))
sreg <- freq(sellers, region)
tbl(sreg, n = 8, caption = "Sellers by region")
```

`seller_id` is unique. Sellers are even more concentrated than customers: `r sreg$region[1]` hosts **`r sreg$pct[1]`%** of them. All `r n_distinct(sellers$region)` seller regions also appear among the `r n_distinct(customers$region)` customer regions.

```{r se-activity}
seller_act <- items %>% distinct() %>% group_by(seller_id) %>%
  summarise(item_lines = n(), orders = n_distinct(order_id), revenue = sum(item_price))
top10 <- seller_act %>% arrange(desc(revenue)) %>% slice(1:ceiling(n() * 0.1))
tbl(numeric_summary(select(seller_act, item_lines, orders, revenue)), caption = "Activity per seller")
```

Seller activity has a very long tail. The top 10% of sellers generate **`r round(100 * sum(top10$revenue) / sum(seller_act$revenue), 1)`%** of item revenue, while `r fmt(sum(seller_act$orders == 1))` sellers (`r pct(sum(seller_act$orders == 1), nrow(seller_act))`) have a single order. Seller-level estimates for small sellers will be noisy.

# payments

```{r pa-structure}
tbl(profile_columns(payments), caption = "Column profile")
tbl(bind_rows(key_info(payments, "order_id"), key_info(payments, c("order_id", "payment_sequence"))))
pay_per_order <- payments %>% count(order_id, name = "payments")
```

The key is (`order_id`, `payment_sequence`). `r pct(sum(pay_per_order$payments > 1), nrow(pay_per_order))` of orders are split over several payments, up to `r max(pay_per_order$payments)`, so **payments must be summed per order** before joining.

## Methods, instalments and amounts

```{r pa-methods}
tbl(payments %>% group_by(payment_method) %>%
      summarise(payments = n(), pct = round(100 * n() / nrow(payments), 2),
                min_inst = min(installments), mean_inst = mean(installments), max_inst = max(installments),
                zero_amount = sum(payment_amount == 0)) %>% arrange(desc(payments)))
tbl(numeric_summary(select(payments, installments, payment_amount)))
```

Only CARD payments use instalments. Small anomalies: `r sum(payments$installments == 0)` payments with **0 instalments**, `r sum(payments$payment_amount == 0)` with **amount 0**, and `r sum(payments$payment_method == "UNKNOWN")` with method **UNKNOWN**.

## Do payments add up to item price + freight?

```{r pa-recon}
paid <- payments %>% group_by(order_id) %>% summarise(paid = sum(payment_amount))
due  <- items %>% distinct() %>% group_by(order_id) %>% summarise(due = sum(item_price + freight_cost))
due_raw <- items %>% group_by(order_id) %>% summarise(due_raw = sum(item_price + freight_cost))
recon <- inner_join(paid, due, by = "order_id") %>% left_join(due_raw, by = "order_id") %>%
  mutate(diff = paid - due, diff_raw = paid - due_raw)

dup_orders <- items %>% filter(duplicated(items)) %>% distinct(order_id)
rd <- recon %>% semi_join(dup_orders, by = "order_id")
tbl(tibble(orders_with_duplicate_item_rows = nrow(rd),
           payment_matches_deduplicated_total = sum(abs(rd$diff) <= 1),
           payment_matches_raw_total = sum(abs(rd$diff_raw) <= 1)),
    caption = "Which total do payments match for orders with duplicated item rows?")

mism <- recon %>% filter(abs(diff) > 1) %>% mutate(ratio = paid / due) %>%
  left_join(payments %>% group_by(order_id) %>% summarise(max_inst = max(installments)), by = "order_id")
tbl(mism %>% mutate(ratio_band = cut(ratio, c(0, 0.9, 0.99, 1.1, 2, 9.99, 10.01, Inf),
                                     labels = c("<0.90", "0.90-0.99", "1.01-1.10", "1.10-2", "2-9.99",
                                                "exactly 10x", ">10x"))) %>%
      group_by(ratio_band) %>%
      summarise(orders = n(), share_card_with_instalments = mean(max_inst > 1)),
    caption = "Orders where paid ≠ due (by more than 1 unit), by paid/due ratio")
ten_x <- sum(abs(mism$ratio - 10) < 0.01)
```

- **Payments match item + freight for `r pct(sum(abs(recon$diff) <= 1), nrow(recon))` of orders** once duplicate item rows are removed. For every order with a duplicated item row, the payment matches the de-duplicated total and never the raw one. This confirms the duplicates are errors.
- **`r ten_x` orders were paid exactly 10× the amount due**, a likely decimal-point error.
- Most other overpayments (1–100% above the total) are on card payments with instalments. That is consistent with instalment interest, so they are probably legitimate.

# customer_feedback

```{r fb-structure}
tbl(profile_columns(feedback), caption = "Column profile")
tbl(bind_rows(key_info(feedback, "feedback_id"), key_info(feedback, "order_id"),
              key_info(feedback, c("feedback_id", "order_id"))))
```

## Feedback and orders are many-to-many

```{r fb-keys}
fid_multi <- feedback %>% group_by(feedback_id) %>% filter(n() > 1) %>%
  summarise(rows = n(), orders = n_distinct(order_id), ratings = n_distinct(rating))
oid_multi <- feedback %>% group_by(order_id) %>% filter(n() > 1) %>%
  summarise(rows = n(), ratings = n_distinct(rating))
```

Neither `feedback_id` nor `order_id` is unique on its own; only the pair is.

- `r nrow(fid_multi)` feedback IDs appear on several rows. They always point to *different* orders with the *same* rating, so one feedback can cover several orders.
- **`r nrow(oid_multi)` orders have more than one feedback record, and `r sum(oid_multi$ratings > 1)` of them have conflicting ratings.** Before joining ratings to orders we need a rule, for example keeping the latest record or the average.

## Ratings

```{r fb-rating, fig.height = 3}
rating_status <- feedback %>% left_join(select(orders, order_id, order_status), by = "order_id") %>%
  group_by(order_status) %>%
  summarise(feedback = n(), mean_rating = mean(rating), pct_rating_1_2 = 100 * mean(rating <= 2)) %>%
  arrange(desc(feedback))
ggplot(count(feedback, rating), aes(factor(rating), n)) +
  geom_col(fill = col_main, width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = 0.1)), vjust = -0.4, colour = ink, size = 3.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .12))) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of ratings", subtitle = "J-shaped: mostly 5s, with a second peak at 1",
       x = "Rating", y = "Feedback records")
tbl(rating_status, caption = "Ratings by status of the reviewed order")
```

The mean rating (`r round(mean(feedback$rating), 2)`) hides a **J-shaped distribution**. Rating is better treated as ordinal, or as a binary "low rating" (1–2), than as a normally distributed continuous outcome. Fulfilment is strongly linked to satisfaction: completed orders average `r round(rating_status$mean_rating[rating_status$order_status == "COMPLETED"], 2)`, and every other status averages 2.5 or less.

## Text indicators

```{r fb-text}
tbl(count(feedback, has_comment, comment_length_positive = comment_length > 0), caption = "has_comment vs comment_length")
tbl(feedback %>% group_by(rating) %>%
      summarise(n = n(), pct_with_comment = 100 * mean(has_comment), mean_comment_length = mean(comment_length)),
    caption = "Comments by rating")
```

`has_comment` is fully consistent with `comment_length`. Unhappy customers write much more often: about three quarters of 1-star ratings carry a comment, against about a third of 4–5-star ratings.

## Timing

```{r fb-timing}
fbo <- feedback %>% left_join(select(orders, order_id, purchase_timestamp, delivery_timestamp), by = "order_id") %>%
  mutate(answer_days = as.numeric(difftime(feedback_answered_timestamp, feedback_created_timestamp, units = "days")))
tbl(feedback %>% count(time_of_day = format(feedback_created_timestamp, "%H:%M:%S"),
                       month = format(feedback_created_timestamp, "%m")) %>%
      group_by(time_of_day) %>% summarise(records = sum(n), months = paste(unique(month), collapse = ", ")),
    caption = "Time of day of feedback creation")
before_purchase <- sum(as.Date(fbo$feedback_created_timestamp) < as.Date(fbo$purchase_timestamp), na.rm = TRUE)
before_delivery <- sum(as.Date(fbo$feedback_created_timestamp) < as.Date(fbo$delivery_timestamp), na.rm = TRUE)
tbl(numeric_summary(select(fbo, answer_days)), caption = "Days from feedback creation to answer")
```

- Feedback creation is recorded as a **date**. `r sum(format(feedback$feedback_created_timestamp, "%H") == "01")` records show 01:00, all in the same month, which looks like a timezone or DST artifact.
- **`r before_purchase` feedback records are dated before the purchase**, which is impossible.
- `r fmt(before_delivery)` (`r pct(before_delivery, nrow(fbo))`) are dated before delivery. These may be complaints about late orders, which matters for any "delay → rating" analysis.
- Feedback is answered after a median of `r round(median(fbo$answer_days), 1)` days, with a maximum of `r round(max(fbo$answer_days))` days.

# Relationships and join behaviour

## Referential integrity

```{r rel-fk}
fk <- bind_rows(
  check_fk(orders,   "orders",      customers, "customers", "customer_record_id"),
  check_fk(items,    "order_items", orders,    "orders",    "order_id"),
  check_fk(items,    "order_items", products,  "products",  "product_id"),
  check_fk(items,    "order_items", sellers,   "sellers",   "seller_id"),
  check_fk(payments, "payments",    orders,    "orders",    "order_id"),
  check_fk(feedback, "customer_feedback", orders, "orders", "order_id"))
tbl(fk)
```

*`unmatched_rows`* are child rows that would be lost in an inner join. *`parents_without_child`* are parent keys with no matching child row. **`r fk$unmatched_keys[3]` product IDs are sold but missing from `products`.** Every other foreign key resolves.

```{r rel-coverage}
tbl(orders %>% mutate(has_items = order_id %in% items$order_id, has_payment = order_id %in% payments$order_id,
                      has_feedback = order_id %in% feedback$order_id) %>%
      group_by(order_status) %>%
      summarise(orders = n(), no_items = sum(!has_items), no_payment = sum(!has_payment),
                no_feedback = sum(!has_feedback)) %>% arrange(desc(orders)),
    caption = "Orders without matching child rows, by status")
```

Orders without items are almost entirely UNAVAILABLE or CANCELLED. One completed order has no payment record, and `r sum(!orders$order_id %in% feedback$order_id)` orders have no feedback. An inner join to feedback would therefore silently drop them, and that is a possible selection issue.

## Cardinality and fan-out

```{r rel-card}
card <- function(x, key) { k <- count(x, .data[[key]]); tibble(min = min(k$n), mean = mean(k$n), max = max(k$n)) }
tbl(bind_rows(
  tibble(join = "customer_record_id in customers") %>% bind_cols(card(customers, "customer_record_id")),
  tibble(join = "customer_id in customers") %>% bind_cols(card(customers, "customer_id")),
  tibble(join = "order_id in order_items") %>% bind_cols(card(items, "order_id")),
  tibble(join = "order_id in payments") %>% bind_cols(card(payments, "order_id")),
  tibble(join = "order_id in customer_feedback") %>% bind_cols(card(feedback, "order_id")),
  tibble(join = "product_id in order_items") %>% bind_cols(card(items, "product_id")),
  tibble(join = "seller_id in order_items") %>% bind_cols(card(items, "seller_id"))),
  caption = "Rows per key value")

j1 <- orders %>% left_join(items, by = "order_id", relationship = "many-to-many")
j2 <- j1 %>% left_join(payments, by = "order_id", relationship = "many-to-many")
j3 <- j2 %>% left_join(feedback, by = "order_id", relationship = "many-to-many")
naive_rev <- sum(j3$payment_amount, na.rm = TRUE); true_rev <- sum(payments$payment_amount)
tbl(tibble(step = c("orders", "+ order_items", "+ payments", "+ customer_feedback"),
           rows = c(nrow(orders), nrow(j1), nrow(j2), nrow(j3)),
           distinct_orders = c(n_distinct(orders$order_id), n_distinct(j1$order_id),
                               n_distinct(j2$order_id), n_distinct(j3$order_id))),
    caption = "Naive join of the order-level tables")
```

Joining the tables directly multiplies rows. `r fmt(nrow(orders))` orders become `r fmt(nrow(j3))` rows, and **summing `payment_amount` afterwards overstates revenue by `r pct(naive_rev - true_rev, true_rev)`** (`r fmt(round(naive_rev))` vs `r fmt(round(true_rev))`). Each table must be aggregated to the chosen unit of observation *before* joining.

# Key findings

1.  **Different units of observation.** `order_items`, `payments` and `customer_feedback` all have several rows per order. Naive joins inflate payment totals by `r pct(naive_rev - true_rev, true_rev)`.
2.  **Customer identity.** `customer_record_id` is one record per order. The real person is `customer_id`, and `r pct(n_multi, nrow(rec_per_cust))` of people have several records.
3.  **Duplicate item lines.** There are `r n_exact` exact duplicates in `order_items`, which payments confirm are errors.
4.  **Category labels.** There are `r nrow(cat_map)` raw labels for `r n_distinct(cat_map$normalised)` real categories, and `r sum(is.na(products$product_category))` products have no category or listing metadata.
5.  **Implausible product weights.** There are `r big` values over 100 kg in small boxes (up to 9.4 t), plus `r sum(products$weight_g == 0, na.rm = TRUE)` zero weights.
6.  **Order timeline.** `r fmt(seq_checks$orders[2])` orders reach the carrier before approval, and delivery estimates are dates rather than date-times (`r pct(late_date, 1)` late by date).
7.  **Payments mostly reconcile** (`r pct(sum(abs(recon$diff) <= 1), nrow(recon))`). `r ten_x` orders were paid exactly 10× the amount due, and there are small anomalies (0 instalments, 0 amounts, UNKNOWN method).
8.  **Feedback is many-to-many with orders.** `r sum(oid_multi$ratings > 1)` orders carry conflicting ratings, and `r before_purchase` feedback records predate the purchase.
9.  **Ratings are J-shaped and strongly related to fulfilment status**, so they suit ordinal or binary modelling.
10. **Coverage gaps.** `r sum(!orders$order_id %in% items$order_id)` orders have no items, `r length(setdiff(unique(items$product_id), products$product_id))` sold products are missing from `products`, and the first and last months are sparse.
